extracted.intended_audience: readers and creators of American literature, artists, and orators (writers, painters, critics interested in an Americanist aesthetic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and aesthetic criteria for producing literature, poetry, painting, and oratory rooted in the American West (prairies, plains, Mississippi valley, Rocky Mountains). Emphasizes indigenous material, landscape study, and forms adapted to democratic audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctively American literature (rooted, not derivative)
rubrics_metrics.description: "a perfect poem, or other esthetic work, entirely western, fresh and limitless--altogether our own, without a trace or taste of Europe's soil, reminiscence, technical letter or spirit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman insists literature worthy of the nation must be born of American landscapes and conditions rather than copied from British models; he repeatedly argues that imported poets and traditions are foreign and inadequate for expressing the Prairies, Plains, and Mississippi Valley. The pages advise waiting until native materials and experiences (the West, prairies, rivers) are assimilated into art rather than relying on European 'models and lay-figures.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature will follow material foundations (timing and precedence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our work at present is to lay the foundations of a great nation in products, in agriculture, in commerce, in networks of intercommunication... When those have their results and get settled, then a literature worthy of us will begin to be defined."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman treats material development—prosperity, intercommunication (railroads, telegraphs), and broad-based social conditions—as prerequisites for a mature national literature. This is prescriptive about timing: cultural production of the appropriate sort will emerge after economic and infrastructural consolidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Plains/Mississippi region as concrete background
rubrics_metrics.description: "the Plains, the Prairies, and the Mississippi river, with the demesnes of its varied and ample valley, should be the concrete background" for the new American imaginative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He urges writers and artists to make the immense central landscapes (prairies, Mississippi system) the literal setting and source material for American narratives and imagery—treating them as the national milieu that will supply people, passions, struggles, and ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: The average bulk of the people, not isolated geniuses, defines national character
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our American superiority and vitality are in the bulk of our people, not in a gentry like the old world... We will not have great individuals or great leaders, but a great average bulk."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman recommends that national literature capture and reflect the mass character, experiences, and common life of ordinary people rather than focusing on singular, exceptional figures; this is a criterion for theme and subject-matter selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artists should 'feed' on Western landscapes before producing New-World art
rubrics_metrics.description: "the chyle of not only poetry and painting... need first and feeding visits here."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He prescribes direct, experiential study trips to the West (prairies, mountains, parks) as essential preparatory work for artists and poets: observation and immersion in local nature are necessary inputs before producing authentic American art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study mountain streams as a unique artistic subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "The spiritual contrast and etheriality of the whole region consist largely to me in its never-absent peculiar streams... The shapes that element takes in the shows of the globe cannot be fully understood by an artist until he has studied these unique rivulets."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman singles out mountain streams as a distinctive formal subject for landscape art: their forms, cascades, and the effects of snowmelt create shapes and moods different from pastoral streams and require direct study to be represented authentically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study aerial effects (transparent lilacs and grays) and novel color gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everywhere the aerial gradations and sky-effects inimitable; nowhere else such perspectives, such transparent lilacs and grays."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He calls attention to specific atmospheric/color phenomena of the West—unique sky-hues, misty lilacs, delicate varicolors on rocks—that painters and colorists should observe and use. The passage functions as practical stylistic guidance for palette and treatment of light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prairies and plains provide enduring esthetic value (duration over spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "While less stunning at first sight, last longer, fill the esthetic sense fuller, precede all the rest, and make North America's characteristic landscape."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman argues that artists should value and represent the subtle, lasting emotional power of broad plains and prairies—these landscapes offer sustained aesthetic effect and cultural centrality, even if not as immediately dramatic as waterfalls or geysers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oratory adapted to American democracy: face-to-face, plain, opportunely fashioned
rubrics_metrics.description: "They are shrewd, good-natur'd, face-to-face speeches, on easy topics not too deep... I hear them criticised as wanting in dignity, but to me they are just what they should be, considering all the circumstances... Underneath, his objects are to compact and fraternize the States, encourage their materialistic and industrial development..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman presents a model for political speaking appropriate to democratic, western audiences: impromptu, conversational, accessible, and practically aimed at social cohesion and development. Dignified classical forms are not required; effectiveness and fraternization are the evaluative measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape composition: foreground-to-horizon perspective and variety of forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "every rood a new view flashing... on the almost perpendicular sides, clinging pines, cedars, spruces, crimson sumach bushes, spots of wild grass--but dominating all, those towering rocks...fantastic forms, bathed in transparent browns, faint reds and grays..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific compositional elements Whitman elevates for landscape depiction: frequent changing views, strong foreground detail (trees, bushes, grass), dominant monumental rock-forms, and colorful variegation. Use rapid alternation of vistas and emphasize contrasts of scale and color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject imported poetic models when they fail to fit local reality
rubrics_metrics.description: "all the prevalent book and library poets, either as imported from Great Britain, or follow'd and doppel-gang'd here, are foreign to our States... they are foreign to our States, copiously as they are read by us all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whitman advises that reliance on British poetic conventions yields misfit and anachronism in American contexts; creators should avoid merely imitating imported forms whose subjects, sensibilities, and scale do not match American landscapes and life.
